docs.title: imzy
docs.text:
Read, inspect, process, and export imaging mass spectrometry datasets from Python. imzy provides a common reader interface for imzML, Bruker TSF/TDF/NeoFlex, and Waters MassLynx data.

pip install imzy

from imzy import get_reader

reader = get_reader("sample.imzML")
mzs, intensities = reader.get_spectrum(0)
image = reader.get_ion_image(734.569, ppm=10, silent=True)

Start with installation and the quickstart, which creates its own sample dataset. The user guide explains spectra and images, and the examples provide runnable scripts. Use the API reference for parameters, defaults, and return shapes.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Read individual spectra, iterate pixels, and sum spectra over selected pixels.
  • Extract single or multiple ion images with Da or ppm windows.
  • Calculate normalization multipliers and export mass-targeted tables to HDF5 or Zarr.
  • Convert supported inputs to imzML through Python or the command line.
  • Choose the Rust or Python imzML backend.

See performance methodology, the recorded backend comparison, and interactive benchmark history.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
imzy is released under the BSD 3-Clause License. Report bugs on GitHub. See the repository's contribution guide and security policy.

These docs track main. A released PyPI version can differ from the current development version.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: Import public objects from imzy. This reference covers the main workflows; backend SDK internals are outside the public reader interface. PathLike below means a string or a filesystem path accepted by the reader.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
get_reader(path: PathLike, **kwargs) -> BaseReader

Detects a built-in or installed plugin reader. Extra keyword arguments are forwarded to that reader. Unsupported inputs raise an error. Vendor readers are available only on their supported platforms.

docs.title: Constructors
docs.text:
IMZMLReader(
    path, ibd_path=None, auto_profile=True, mz_ppm="auto", resolution=50_000,
    mz_min=None, mz_max=None, parse_lib=None, *, backend="auto",
)
TSFReader(path, use_recalibrated_state=False, auto_profile=True, roi=None)
TDFReader(
    path, use_recalibrated_state=False,
    pressure_compensation_strategy=PressureStrategy.NoCompensation, roi=None,
)
NeoFlexReader(path, use_recalibrated_state=False, auto_profile=True, resolution=30_000, roi=None)
WatersReader(path, auto_profile=True, mz_ppm="auto", resolution="auto", enable_ion_mobility=True)

Each constructor returns its corresponding BaseReader subclass. ibd_path overrides the imzML binary-file location; otherwise the matching .ibd is used. mz_min / mz_max override imzML mass-range estimates. parse_lib selects the XML parser; leave it as None for automatic selection. backend accepts "auto", "rust", or "python". resolution and mz_ppm control centroid resampling; their defaults are estimates, not instrument calibration. auto_profile controls automatic centroid-to-profile conversion where the reader implements it. Bruker roi=None uses the reader's default region selection; an integer selects a reported ROI. use_recalibrated_state requests the vendor recalibration state. TDF pressure compensation uses the PressureStrategy enum in imzy._readers.bruker._tdf and defaults to no compensation. Waters enable_ion_mobility defaults to enabled.

IMZMLReader supports with ... as reader and close() -> None. Its backend property reports "python" or "rust". Closing prevents further reads; returned native arrays can retain the mapping. See backend lifetime.

docs.title: Shared spectra and image operations
docs.text:
These signatures describe the common usage supported by the built-in readers. Output arrays are NumPy arrays.

Method Return value / behavior get_spectrum(index: int) (mzs, intensities), two 1-D arrays; indices are zero-based get_intensities(index: int) 1-D intensity array for one pixel spectra_iter(indices=None, silent=False) Iterator of (mzs, intensities) pairs; None selects all pixels get_summed_spectrum(indices, scales=None, silent=False) (mzs, summed_intensities); indices must be nonempty; scales has one multiplier per original pixel get_tic(silent=False) Cached total-ion-current vector, shape (n_pixels,) get_ion_image(mz, tol=None, ppm=None, fill_value=np.nan, silent=False) One image, shape (height, width) get_ion_images(mzs, tol=None, ppm=None, fill_value=np.nan, silent=False) Image stack, shape (n_masses, height, width) to_table(mzs, tol=None, ppm=None, fill_value=np.nan, silent=False) Flat intensity table, shape (n_pixels, n_masses) reshape(array, fill_value=0) Place (n_pixels,) values into a (height, width) image reshape_batch(array, fill_value=0) Convert (n_pixels, n_masses) to (n_masses, height, width) flatten(array) Retrieve acquired pixels from a 2-D image, shape (n_pixels,)

Mass extraction takes exactly one positive tol (Da half-width) or ppm (relative half-width). fill_value describes unacquired image positions. Centroid summation uses resampling and can produce a different mass grid from individual spectra.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Value path Input dataset path n_pixels, pixels Acquired-pixel count and original pixel indices image_shape (height, width) xyz_coordinates (n_pixels, 3) coordinates in reader convention x_coordinates, y_coordinates, z_coordinates Per-pixel coordinate vectors mz_min, mz_max Reader mass-range bounds is_centroid Whether the input is centroid data rois Available ROI identifiers x_pixel_size, y_pixel_size Physical pixel sizes where supplied by the input

Use reader reshape methods to account for coordinate origin and missing pixels.

docs.title: Normalization and extraction
docs.text:
get_normalizations() -> list[str]
reader.get_normalizations(silent=False) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
reader.extract_normalizations_hdf5(hdf_path, silent=False) -> Path
reader.to_hdf5(
    hdf_path, mzs, tol=None, ppm=None, as_flat=True, max_mem=512, silent=False,
) -> Path
reader.to_zarr(
    zarr_path, mzs, tol=None, ppm=None, as_flat=True, chunk_size=None, silent=False,
) -> Path

The module function lists supported names; the reader method calculates (n_pixels,) multiplier arrays. extract_normalizations_hdf5() persists factors, reusing an existing file. Storage exports require a nonempty mass list and the corresponding optional extra. Only flat tables are supported. HDF5 max_mem is in MB; Zarr chunk_size is (pixels, masses). See normalization and storage for examples and output reuse behavior.

docs.title: Writers
docs.text:
write_imzml(
    reader, output_path, *, ibd_mode="auto", spectrum_type="auto", coordinate_origin="auto",
    mz_dtype=None, intensity_dtype=None, on_error="error", overwrite=False, indices=None,
    source_path=None, pixel_size=None, image_shape=None, normalization=None,
    spectrum_transform=None, silent=False,
) -> Path

IMZMLWriter(
    output_path, *, mz_dtype=np.float64, intensity_dtype=np.float32, ibd_mode="auto",
    spectrum_type="centroid", polarity=None, coordinate_origin="one", on_error="error",
    overwrite=False, source_path=None, pixel_size=None, image_shape=None,
)

write_imzml() returns the output .imzML path. IMZMLWriter.from_reader() accepts the same parameters and returns the same result. The manual constructor returns a writer; always close it or use a context manager.

  • ibd_mode: "auto", "continuous", or "processed". Auto selects continuous for profile and processed for centroid.
  • spectrum_type: "centroid" or "profile"; reader conversion additionally accepts "auto".
  • coordinate_origin: "zero", "one", or "auto". In reader conversion, auto uses the reader format. On the manual writer, explicit auto is treated as zero; the manual default is one.
  • mz_dtype, intensity_dtype: float32, float64, int32, or int64; conversion with None uses reader precision when available.
  • on_error: "error" or "warn". Empty spectra always warn and skip.
  • indices: original pixel indices to export; None means all.
  • source_path, pixel_size, image_shape: source metadata, (x_size, y_size) physical pixel size, and (height, width) image size. Conversion inherits them from the reader when omitted.
  • normalization: multiplier name, or None. spectrum_transform is an optional (index, mzs, intensities) -> (mzs, intensities) callback applied after normalization.
  • polarity: "positive" or "negative", or None for unspecified.
writer.add_spectrum(mzs, intensities, coords, user_params=None, *, error_context=None) -> bool
writer.close() -> None

add_spectrum() accepts matching 1-D arrays and (x, y) / (x, y, z) coordinates. It returns whether the spectrum was written. user_params accepts mappings with required name and value entries. error_context adds context to skip warnings. close() finalizes output. Existing files raise FileExistsError unless overwrite is enabled.

Warnings exported from imzy: IMZMLWriterWarning, SkippedSpectrumWarning, EmptySpectrumWarning. The latter two specialize skipped-spectrum reporting. See writing for mode constraints.

docs.title: Storage classes
docs.text:
H5CentroidsStore(path, xyz_coordinates=None, pixel_index=None, image_shape=None, mode="a")
ZarrCentroidsStore(path, xyz_coordinates=None, pixel_index=None, image_shape=None)
H5NormalizationStore(path, mode="a")
InMemoryStore(reader, xyz_coordinates=None, pixel_index=None, image_shape=None)

HDF5 and Zarr centroid stores expose xs (stored mass axis) and n_peaks (mass count):

Method Result get_ion(value: int \| float) (n_pixels,); integer column index or nearest float mass get_ions(mzs: np.ndarray) (n_pixels, n_masses) table for nearest stored masses get_ion_indices(xs: np.ndarray) (matched_masses, column_indices)

Zarr get_ions(mzs, filtered=False) can select a pre-existing filtered table; requesting missing filtered data raises ValueError. For images, use reader.reshape() / reshape_batch() with the stored vectors/tables. HDF5 store methods manage their file access internally; mode="r" requests read access. Zarr opens a group in append mode.

InMemoryStore delegates extraction to a reader: get_ion(mz, fill_value=np.nan, ppm=3.0) returns a 2-D image and get_ions(mzs, fill_value=np.nan, ppm=3.0) returns a 3-D stack. Unlike persisted stores, it extracts from the source for each call.

H5NormalizationStore.get_normalization_list() -> list[str] lists stored names. get_normalization(name, as_median=True, as_multiplier=True) returns a stored (n_pixels,) factor array; the two flags currently do not alter retrieval. store[name] is equivalent. normalize(array, name, **kwargs) applies multipliers to a vector or a flat (n_pixels, n_masses) table.

docs.title: Reader plugins
docs.text:
Register a package module through the imzy.plugins entry point. Implement the imzy_reader hook, decorated with imzy.hookspec.hook_impl, returning a BaseReader for supported paths and None otherwise:

from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from imzy import BaseReader
from imzy.hookspec import hook_impl


@hook_impl
def imzy_reader(path: str | Path, **kwargs: Any) -> BaseReader | None:
    """Return a reader for this plugin's supported format."""
    if Path(path).suffix != ".yourformat":
        return None
    # Implement YourReader as a BaseReader subclass in your package.
    return YourReader(path, **kwargs)

[project.entry-points."imzy.plugins"]
your_project_name = "your_project_name.imzy"

This is an extension-point sketch: YourReader must implement spectrum access, metadata, coordinates, and any advertised operations. get_reader() loads the registered plugins automatically.

docs.title: Rust imzML backend
docs.text:
The imzML reader supports memory-mapped Rust access and a Python fallback behind the same reader interface. The XML parser and metadata cache remain in Python.

from imzy import IMZMLReader

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML", backend="auto") as reader:
    print(reader.backend)
    mzs, intensities = reader.get_spectrum(0)
    writable_intensities = intensities.copy()
Selection Behavior backend="auto" Use Rust when the extension loads, otherwise Python backend="rust" Require Rust; raise ImportError when the extension cannot load backend="python" Explicitly use Python

Auto selection is a fallback for extension availability; malformed data still raises errors. Release wheels include the extension. See source installation when compiling locally. After editing Rust sources, reinstall the package to rebuild the extension.

docs.title: Arrays and file lifetime
docs.text:
Returned spectrum arrays are read-only. Aligned native arrays can be views into the file; unaligned arrays are copied safely. Use .copy() when you need writable data.

Keep input files unchanged while a reader, array, or iterator exists. close() releases the reader's mapping, but native arrays and iterators retain their own mappings. They may keep file locks alive on Windows after the reader closes. Release those references before replacing the dataset.

docs.title: Supported arrays and parallelism
docs.text:
Supported imzML arrays are uncompressed, little-endian float32, float64, int32, and int64. Ion extraction requires ascending m/z arrays. Rust accelerates spectrum access/iteration, TIC calculation, and ion-image extraction. Rayon parallelizes bulk extraction. Set the worker count before starting Python:

RAYON_NUM_THREADS=2 python analysis.py

On PowerShell, set $env:RAYON_NUM_THREADS = "2" before starting Python. See benchmark methodology for the controlled thread settings used in CI, and the recorded comparison for measured workloads and limitations.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Installing imzy adds the imzy command. Convert a supported dataset to imzML:

imzy convert path/to/input path/to/output --silent

The output path may be a base name or an .imzML filename. Both XML and binary files are written. The command prints the resulting imzML path.

imzy convert sample.imzML normalized \
  --normalization TIC \
  --spectrum-type auto \
  --ibd-mode auto

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Accepted values / behavior --spectrum-type auto auto, centroid, profile --ibd-mode auto auto, continuous, processed --normalization NAME None A name returned by Python's imzy.get_normalizations(); case-insensitive --roi INTEGER None Bruker TSF/TDF/NeoFlex ROI ID --overwrite / --no-overwrite No overwrite Replace existing output files when enabled --on-error error error stops conversion; warn skips unreadable/invalid spectra with warnings --silent / --progress Progress Hide or show progress bars

For Bruker input on a supported platform:

imzy convert sample.d roi_export --roi 0

Choose an ROI ID exposed by the dataset. Other formats reject --roi. TDF conversion prints a warning that ion mobility is collapsed to the m/z axis. Empty spectra are skipped with warnings, as described in writing imzML.

imzy --help
imzy convert --help

The Python API additionally supports selecting pixel indices, coordinate origin, output precision, metadata overrides, and custom spectrum transforms.

docs.title: Build and preview
docs.text:
From a repository checkout, install only the existing docs group into a separate environment:

uv venv .asv/docs-env --python 3.12
uv pip install --python .asv/docs-env/bin/python --group docs
.asv/docs-env/bin/python -m mkdocs serve

Open the local URL printed by MkDocs. On Windows, use .asv/docs-env/Scripts/python.exe in place of .asv/docs-env/bin/python. A strict production build is:

.asv/docs-env/bin/python -m mkdocs build --strict

Generated documentation is written to the ignored site/ directory. The build does not import imzy or require a Rust compiler or vendor SDK. Benchmark reports and downloadable example scripts are included from their repository sources by a small MkDocs hook. Edit those original files to update their published versions. Run commands from the repository root so example snippet paths resolve.

docs.title: Examples and checks
docs.text:
Use a separate package environment for tests and examples:

uv venv .asv/examples-env --python 3.12
uv pip install --python .asv/examples-env/bin/python ".[test]"
.asv/examples-env/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_docs.py tests/test_benchmark_history.py

The tests use temporary datasets and check pixel intensities, image shapes, normalization multipliers, conversion round trips, optional storage read-back, and combined-site assembly. Plot tests save PNGs without opening a window. Install the relevant extras when running storage examples separately.

docs.title: GitHub Pages
docs.text:
Documentation and ASV charts are published together by the existing Benchmarks workflow. Pull requests build docs strictly and run correctness and benchmark smoke checks without deploying. Main pushes, the weekly schedule, and manual main runs publish only after checks and measurements succeed. Docs dependencies are installed separately from the pinned benchmark environment.

The deployment layout is:

URL under https://vandeplaslab.github.io/imzy/ Content / MkDocs documentation benchmarks/ Interactive ASV charts and assets asv-results.tar.gz Durable raw history archive at its original URL

In repository Settings > Pages, select GitHub Actions as the source. For an initial deployment, follow the benchmark initialization instructions. When migrating an existing benchmark site, leave initialization disabled: its root archive is restored and retained. Recovery artifact paths and archive validation remain unchanged.

To preview the combined artifact after a local ASV publication and history pack:

.asv/docs-env/bin/python -m mkdocs build --strict
python scripts/build_docs_site.py --docs site --benchmarks .asv/html --output .asv/site
python -m http.server 8000 --directory .asv/site

Assembly requires a fresh output directory. Remove only the generated .asv/site directory before repeating it. Open http://localhost:8000/ for docs and /benchmarks/ for charts. The navigation link to live charts targets the published site. For ASV setup, measurement methodology, archive creation, and recovery, use the benchmark guide.

docs.title: Runnable examples
docs.text: These scripts generate their own two-by-two imzML data. No external datasets or notebook runtime is required. Run commands from a repository checkout, or download both scripts into the same directory and omit examples/ from the commands. Use a fresh output directory for each run to avoid replacing previous data.

docs.title: Spectra, images, and conversion
docs.text:
pip install "imzy[plot]"
python examples/quickstart.py /tmp/imzy-quickstart --plot

On Windows, use an output path such as example-output/quickstart. Omit --plot to run without Matplotlib. The script writes sample.imzML / sample.ibd, normalized.imzML / normalized.ibd, and optionally quickstart.png.

The input spectra contain [1, 2, 3] multiplied by pixel numbers 1 through 4. The TIC vector is [6, 12, 18, 24]; the m/z 200 image is [[2, 4], [6, 8]]. TIC factors scale each spectrum to a total intensity of 15, the median input TIC. The script reads the normalized output back to check this result.

Download quickstart.py.

"""Generate portable IMS data, extract images, normalize, and round-trip an export."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from imzy import IMZMLReader, IMZMLWriter, write_imzml


def create_sample(directory: Path) -> Path:
    """Write a two-by-two centroid dataset with three masses and known intensities."""
    directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path = directory / "sample.imzML"
    with IMZMLWriter(path, spectrum_type="centroid", ibd_mode="processed") as writer:
        for index in range(4):
            intensities = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) * (index + 1)
            writer.add_spectrum([100.0, 200.0, 300.0], intensities, (index % 2 + 1, index // 2 + 1))
    return path


def run(directory: Path, *, plot: bool = False) -> Path:
    """Create sample data and a TIC-normalized copy, optionally saving a plot."""
    path = create_sample(directory)
    with IMZMLReader(path) as reader:
        mzs, intensities = reader.get_spectrum(0)
        tic = reader.get_tic(silent=True)
        images = reader.get_ion_images([100.0, 200.0], tol=0.1, silent=True)
        scales = reader.get_normalizations(silent=True)["TIC"]
        normalized = images[1] * reader.reshape(scales)
        output = write_imzml(reader, directory / "normalized.imzML", normalization="TIC", silent=True)

        if plot:
            import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

            fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3))
            axes[0].plot(mzs, intensities)
            axes[0].set(xlabel="m/z", ylabel="Intensity", title="Pixel 0")
            for ax, image, title in zip(
                axes[1:], [reader.reshape(tic), normalized], ["TIC", "TIC-normalized m/z 200"], strict=True
            ):
                artist = ax.imshow(image)
                ax.set(xlabel="x", ylabel="y", title=title)
                fig.colorbar(artist, ax=ax)
            fig.tight_layout()
            fig.savefig(directory / "quickstart.png", dpi=150)
            plt.close(fig)

    with IMZMLReader(output) as converted:
        # Each normalized pixel has the same total intensity for this proportional input.
        np.testing.assert_allclose(converted.get_tic(silent=True), np.full(4, 15.0), rtol=1e-6)
    print(f"Wrote {output}")
    return output


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("output", type=Path, help="Directory for new datasets; use a fresh directory for each run.")
    parser.add_argument("--plot", action="store_true", help="Save quickstart.png (requires imzy[plot]).")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    run(args.output, plot=args.plot)

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Run each backend in a different output directory. HDF5 requires imzy[hdf5]; Zarr requires Python 3.11+ and imzy[zarr].

pip install "imzy[hdf5,zarr]"
python examples/storage.py /tmp/imzy-hdf5 --backend hdf5
python examples/storage.py /tmp/imzy-zarr --backend zarr

Keep quickstart.py alongside storage.py: it supplies the shared sample-data function. The script checks the exported (4, 2) table against known intensities and reshapes it into (2, 2, 2) images.

Download storage.py.

"""Export sample ion tables to HDF5 and Zarr and verify their stored intensities."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from quickstart import create_sample

from imzy import IMZMLReader


def run(directory: Path, *, backend: str) -> Path:
    """Create sample data and verify one optional storage backend against known sums."""
    path = create_sample(directory)
    expected = np.arange(1, 5)[:, None] * np.array([1.0, 2.0])
    with IMZMLReader(path) as reader:
        if backend == "hdf5":
            from imzy import H5CentroidsStore

            output = reader.to_hdf5(directory / "centroids.h5", [100.0, 200.0], tol=0.1, silent=True)
            store = H5CentroidsStore(output, mode="r")
            table = np.column_stack([store.get_ion(100.0), store.get_ion(200.0)])
        elif backend == "zarr":
            from imzy import ZarrCentroidsStore

            output = reader.to_zarr(directory / "centroids.zarr", [100.0, 200.0], tol=0.1, silent=True)
            store = ZarrCentroidsStore(output)
            table = store.get_ions(np.array([100.0, 200.0]))
        else:
            raise ValueError("Choose hdf5 or zarr.")
        np.testing.assert_allclose(table, expected)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(reader.reshape_batch(table), expected.T.reshape(2, 2, 2))
    print(f"Verified {output}: {table.shape}")
    return output


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("output", type=Path, help="Directory for new datasets; use a fresh directory for each run.")
    parser.add_argument("--backend", choices=["hdf5", "zarr"], required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    run(args.output, backend=args.backend)

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text: The repository also contains exploratory notebooks for basic reading and plotting and imzML conversion. Those require your own input data and platform-specific readers. The scripts above are the automated smoke-tested examples.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
imzy requires Python 3.10 or newer. Install it in a virtual environment:

python -m venv .venv
# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install imzy

docs.title: Optional features
docs.text:
Extra Install Purpose HDF5 pip install "imzy[hdf5]" Export and read HDF5 centroid/normalization stores Zarr pip install "imzy[zarr]" Export and read Zarr centroid stores Plotting pip install "imzy[plot]" Plot examples with Matplotlib All pip install "imzy[all]" All features supported on your Python version

Zarr support requires Python 3.11 or newer and Zarr 3 (zarr>3,<4). On Python 3.10, the all and test extras omit Zarr. You can combine extras, for example pip install "imzy[hdf5,plot]".

docs.title: Formats and platforms
docs.text:
Input Windows macOS Linux imzML (.imzML with its .ibd) Yes Yes Yes Bruker TSF/TDF/NeoFlex (.d) Yes No Yes Waters MassLynx (.raw) Yes No No

Vendor formats depend on their native SDKs. Use imzML for the portable examples. Keep the imzML XML and binary .ibd file together. Bruker TDF export collapses ion mobility onto the m/z axis.

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
Release wheels include the Rust imzML extension and need no Rust compiler. Source builds compile the extension when Cargo is available. To require compilation, install the Rust toolchain and run:

IMZY_BUILD_RUST=1 pip install .

To explicitly install without compilation:

IMZY_BUILD_RUST=0 pip install .

On PowerShell, set $env:IMZY_BUILD_RUST = "1" (or "0") before pip install .. Compilation failures are reported. See backend selection for fallback behavior and thread settings.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This example creates a two-by-two imzML dataset, so no vendor data or download is needed. Run it in a writable directory after pip install imzy. Use a new output name when repeating it; the writer refuses to overwrite existing files by default.

docs.title: Create sample data
docs.text:
from imzy import IMZMLWriter

with IMZMLWriter("sample", spectrum_type="centroid", ibd_mode="processed") as writer:
    writer.add_spectrum([100.0, 200.0, 300.0], [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], (1, 1))
    writer.add_spectrum([100.0, 200.0, 300.0], [2.0, 4.0, 6.0], (2, 1))
    writer.add_spectrum([100.0, 200.0, 300.0], [3.0, 6.0, 9.0], (1, 2))
    writer.add_spectrum([100.0, 200.0, 300.0], [4.0, 8.0, 12.0], (2, 2))

This writes sample.imzML and sample.ibd. Writer coordinates are (x, y) and default to a one-based origin.

docs.title: Read spectra and images
docs.text:
from imzy import IMZMLReader

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    mzs, intensities = reader.get_spectrum(0)
    print(mzs)          # [100. 200. 300.]
    print(intensities)  # [1. 2. 3.]

    tic = reader.get_tic(silent=True)  # shape (4,)
    tic_image = reader.reshape(tic)  # shape (2, 2)
    image = reader.get_ion_image(200.0, tol=0.1, silent=True)
    print(image)  # [[2. 4.], [6. 8.]]

    images = reader.get_ion_images([100.0, 200.0], ppm=10, silent=True)
    print(images.shape)  # (2, 2, 2): masses, rows, columns

Pixel indices start at zero. Images use NumPy (y, x) order. Supply exactly one of tol (Da) and ppm. Opening the reader can create a metadata cache next to the input; the XML remains the metadata source.

docs.title: Normalize and convert
docs.text:
from imzy import IMZMLReader, write_imzml

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    scales = reader.get_normalizations(silent=True)["TIC"]
    image = reader.get_ion_image(200.0, tol=0.1, silent=True)
    normalized_image = image * reader.reshape(scales)
    converted = write_imzml(reader, "normalized", normalization="TIC", silent=True)

Normalization values are multipliers. See normalization and storage for batch operations, or run the complete example to generate plots and validate a conversion.

docs.title: Normalization and storage
docs.text: The snippets here use sample.imzML from the quickstart.

docs.title: Normalization multipliers
docs.text:
from imzy import IMZMLReader, get_normalizations

print(get_normalizations())  # supported names; this does not calculate factors

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    normalizations = reader.get_normalizations(silent=True)
    scales = normalizations["TIC"]  # one multiplier per acquired pixel

    image = reader.get_ion_image(200.0, tol=0.1, silent=True)
    normalized_image = image * reader.reshape(scales)

    table = reader.to_table([100.0, 200.0], tol=0.1, silent=True)
    normalized_table = table * scales[:, None]

    mzs, normalized_sum = reader.get_summed_spectrum(reader.pixels, scales=scales, silent=True)

Multiply by the factors; do not divide by them. Factors have shape (n_pixels,), including when you sum a subset of pixels: scales is indexed by the original pixel index. Strategies include TIC, RMS, Median, percentile-filtered TIC, and 0/2/3-norm. Use get_normalizations() for the exact names. For zero-signal or non-finite input, inspect the resulting factors before analysis.

docs.title: HDF5 centroid tables
docs.text:
Install imzy[hdf5]. Exporting extracts the requested mass windows and stores a flat table, not every original spectrum:

from imzy import H5CentroidsStore, IMZMLReader

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    path = reader.to_hdf5("centroids.h5", [100.0, 200.0], tol=0.1, silent=True)
    store = H5CentroidsStore(path, mode="r")
    ion = store.get_ion(200.0)  # (n_pixels,), nearest stored mass
    image = reader.reshape(ion)

max_mem=512 is the default extraction memory budget in MB. Use a fresh output path for each extraction setup: existing HDF5 output may be reused when its stored mass list matches. A reused path is not a request to recompute with new tolerances. Only as_flat=True is supported.

docs.title: Zarr centroid tables
docs.text:
Install imzy[zarr] on Python 3.11 or newer. Exports use Zarr 3:

import numpy as np
from imzy import IMZMLReader, ZarrCentroidsStore

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    path = reader.to_zarr("centroids.zarr", [100.0, 200.0], tol=0.1, silent=True)
    store = ZarrCentroidsStore(path)
    table = store.get_ions(np.array([200.0, 100.0]))  # (n_pixels, 2)
    images = reader.reshape_batch(table)

The default chunk_size=None lets the exporter choose the chunk shape. A supplied tuple describes (pixels_per_chunk, masses_per_chunk); keep individual chunks within the exporter's 512 MiB limit. Only flat export is supported. Store queries select the nearest mass already extracted; they do not re-integrate the source spectra. Pass an integer to get_ion() to select a stored column by index, or a float to select a mass.

docs.title: Persist normalization factors
docs.text:
from imzy import H5NormalizationStore, IMZMLReader

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    path = reader.extract_normalizations_hdf5("normalizations.h5", silent=True)
store = H5NormalizationStore(path, mode="r")
names = store.get_normalization_list()
scales = store.get_normalization("TIC")

This requires the HDF5 extra. An existing normalization file is reused. See the storage example for a complete export and read-back check.

docs.title: Select a reader
docs.text:
get_reader() detects built-in formats and installed reader plugins:

from imzy import get_reader

reader = get_reader("path/to/dataset")
print(reader.n_pixels, reader.image_shape, reader.is_centroid)
mzs, intensities = reader.get_spectrum(0)

Additional keyword arguments are forwarded to the selected reader. Consult the reader reference before passing format-specific options. For imzML, prefer a context manager to release file mappings promptly:

from imzy import IMZMLReader

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML", backend="auto") as reader:
    for mzs, intensities in reader.spectra_iter(indices=[0, 1], silent=True):
        print(float(intensities.sum()))

An individual spectrum is a pair of one-dimensional arrays with matching lengths. Spectrum lengths may vary in processed centroid datasets. Copy read-only arrays before modifying them.

docs.title: Sum selected pixels
docs.text:
with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    selected = reader.pixels[:min(100, reader.n_pixels)]
    mzs, summed = reader.get_summed_spectrum(selected, silent=True)
    average = summed / len(selected)

Select at least one pixel. For centroid imzML, summation resamples onto a profile grid controlled by resolution and mz_ppm; it does not simply concatenate the peaks. Vendor readers also have format-specific centroid-to-profile behavior. In particular, NeoFlex and Waters readers expose auto_profile=False for raw centroid access.

docs.title: Extract ion images
docs.text:
with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    image = reader.get_ion_image(200.0, ppm=10, silent=True)
    images = reader.get_ion_images([100.0, 200.0, 300.0], tol=0.05, silent=True)
    table = reader.to_table([100.0, 200.0, 300.0], tol=0.05, silent=True)
Operation Shape get_tic() (n_pixels,) get_ion_image(...) (height, width) get_ion_images(mzs, ...) (n_masses, height, width) to_table(mzs, ...) (n_pixels, n_masses)

The intensity at each pixel is the sum within the target mass window. tol=0.05 selects a window of mz +/- 0.05 Da; ppm=10 scales its half-width with the target m/z. Use one positive tolerance, and keep input m/z arrays sorted ascending.

Use batch extraction to obtain several masses in one pass. TIC values are cached within a reader; repeated get_tic() calls reuse the calculated vector.

docs.title: Coordinates and missing pixels
docs.text:
image_shape is (height, width). Coordinates describe acquired pixels, which may not fill a rectangular grid. Use reshape() and reshape_batch() instead of reshaping with NumPy: they place data at the recorded coordinates. flatten(image) retrieves acquired pixels in reader order.

import numpy as np

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    tic_image = reader.reshape(reader.get_tic(silent=True), fill_value=np.nan)
    tic_vector = reader.flatten(tic_image)

reshape() defaults to zero for unacquired pixels; ion-image methods default to NaN for those locations. An acquired pixel with no peak in the window contributes zero. imzML coordinates are one-based, while Bruker reader coordinates use a zero-based image origin. Let the reader handle placement.

docs.title: Bruker regions of interest
docs.text:
from imzy import get_reader

reader = get_reader("sample.d")
print(reader.rois)
roi_reader = get_reader("sample.d", roi=0)  # choose an ID reported by reader.rois

ROI selection applies to Bruker TSF/TDF/NeoFlex. The selected reader exposes the pixels for that region. These examples require a supported vendor platform and real input data.

docs.title: Convert a reader
docs.text:
from imzy import IMZMLReader, write_imzml

with IMZMLReader("sample.imzML") as reader:
    output = write_imzml(reader, "converted", normalization="TIC", silent=True)
print(output)  # Path to converted.imzML

Use get_reader() for vendor input. The output is a pair of .imzML and .ibd files. Keep both files together. The writer refuses existing outputs unless overwrite=True.

Option Default Meaning spectrum_type "auto" Infer centroid/profile from the reader, or choose "centroid" / "profile" ibd_mode "auto" Continuous for profile, processed for centroid; can be explicitly selected coordinate_origin "auto" One-based for imzML readers, zero-based for other readers indices None Export every pixel, or supply original zero-based pixel indices normalization None Apply the named normalization multiplier before writing on_error "error" Stop on errors, or use "warn" to skip unreadable/invalid spectra silent False Show progress by default

Continuous mode requires identical m/z arrays for every spectrum. Processed mode permits independent axes. Bruker TDF spectra are collapsed onto m/z when exported; ion mobility is not retained. For readers with centroid-to-profile conversion support, explicitly requesting profile output can resample centroid data; it does not recover a measured profile spectrum.

docs.title: Add spectra manually
docs.text:
from imzy import IMZMLWriter

with IMZMLWriter("manual", spectrum_type="centroid", ibd_mode="processed") as writer:
    writer.add_spectrum([100.0, 101.0], [10.0, 50.0], (1, 1))
    writer.add_spectrum([100.0, 102.0], [20.0, 30.0], (2, 1))

Coordinates are (x, y) or (x, y, z), in imzML axis order, with one-based coordinates by default. Two-dimensional coordinates are written with z=1. Use coordinate_origin="zero" to shift zero-based coordinates by one during export. Arrays must be finite, one-dimensional, and have matching lengths; m/z values must be sorted ascending.

IMZMLWriter defaults to float64 m/z and float32 intensity arrays. write_imzml() preserves reader precision when available, otherwise using those defaults. Supply mz_dtype and intensity_dtype to choose explicitly. Metadata overrides include polarity on the manual writer and pixel_size / image_shape on both interfaces. See the writer reference for the full signatures.

docs.title: Finalization and skipped spectra
docs.text:
Always close the writer, preferably with a context manager. Closing finalizes XML and binary metadata and moves temporary outputs into place. A context manager cleans up temporary files when its body raises an exception. Empty spectra are skipped with EmptySpectrumWarning, including under on_error="error". Other skipped spectra emit SkippedSpectrumWarning when on_error="warn".

add_spectrum() returns True when written and False when skipped. Review warnings when skipping is enabled; the output can contain fewer pixels than the input.

docs.title: Performance benchmarks
docs.text:
Documentation | Interactive results | Raw history archive | ASV documentation

The ASV suite tracks imzy's public reader and export workflows across main revisions. Charts are hosted under /imzy/benchmarks/; documentation occupies the site root. The raw history archive keeps its original root URL. The separate local backend report and scripts/benchmark_imzml.py remain available.

docs.title: Local setup and runs
docs.text:
Use Python 3.12.13 and a Rust compiler. CI pins Rust 1.99.1; install that toolchain to match its compiler. Create a separate environment so benchmarking does not change your normal development dependencies:

uv venv --python 3.12.13 .asv/runner
uv pip install --python .asv/runner/bin/python -r benchmarks/requirements.txt
IMZY_BUILD_RUST=1 uv pip install --python .asv/runner/bin/python --no-deps --no-build-isolation .

export NUMBA_DISABLE_JIT=0 NUMBA_NUM_THREADS=1 RAYON_NUM_THREADS=2
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1

machine=$(.asv/runner/bin/python scripts/benchmark_history.py machine --label local)
.asv/runner/bin/python -m asv check --python=same
.asv/runner/bin/python -m asv run --python=same --quick --dry-run --machine "$machine"

Run these commands from the repository root. Machine registration supports Linux and macOS, matching the initial benchmark hosting target. Both backends and the HDF5/Zarr dependencies are required; unavailable components fail instead of silently dropping cases.

For a full run of the installed checkout, followed by a website preview:

revision=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
.asv/runner/bin/python -m asv run --python=same --set-commit-hash "$revision" --record-samples --machine "$machine"
.asv/runner/bin/python -m asv publish
.asv/runner/bin/python scripts/benchmark_history.py pack
.asv/runner/bin/python -m asv preview

Only label an installed wheel with the revision it was built from. Reinstall it after changing runtime code. For ASV to build a particular committed revision in its own pinned environment, omit --python=same and use a single-revision range:

.asv/runner/bin/python -m asv run "$revision^!" --record-samples --machine "$machine"

Environments, fixtures, results, and generated HTML live under the ignored .asv/ directory. Local results stay local. Do not merge measurements from different machines under the same machine name. Publication charts the branches listed in asv.conf.json, initially main. To preview results from a feature branch, use a temporary local configuration with that branch added to branches; keep the production configuration on main.

docs.title: Workloads and timing methodology
docs.text:
There are 88 parameter combinations: 11 operations, two backends, two layouts, and two pixel counts (256 and 4096). Continuous profile spectra share a float64 m/z axis with 2048 points. Processed centroid spectra have independently sorted float64 axes with 1024-2048 points. Intensities are seeded, varied float32 lognormal values. The data are synthetic; vendor SDK performance and cold-storage throughput are outside this suite.

  • Random access reads up to 1024 seeded pixel indices with replacement. Iteration reads every spectrum. Both consume both complete arrays using the same float64 checksum reduction for each backend.
  • One ion image uses m/z 150. Batch extraction and storage exports use 32 masses between 150 and 950, with a 0.3 Da inclusive tolerance. Timed reads consume the complete output arrays; exports synchronously write complete stores.
  • TIC caching is reset on every timed call. Normalizations compute all supported factors for every pixel.
  • Cached initialization includes reader open and close. Uncached initialization additionally includes XML parsing and metadata-cache creation. Its cache is removed before each sample, outside the timer. Neither claims cold OS caches.
  • Fixture generation, backend loading, Numba warmup, temporary-directory setup, and cleanup are outside the timer. Export timings include extraction, serialization, finalization, and close; Zarr also includes rechunking. They measure writes through the OS page cache, without forcing disk synchronization.
  • Every sample calls its operation once. Three samples in each of two rounds produce six recorded samples per case. Automatic timed warmup is disabled so it cannot populate a TIC or export cache before measurement.
  • Correctness tests use generated spectra and independent NumPy references for ion sums and normalization factors. They also check backend agreement, complete export round trips, and repeated uncached work.

The benchmark requirements file pins the full resolved software environment, including build and test tools. CI fixes Numba/BLAS/OpenMP to one worker and Rayon to two workers. Machine names include a fingerprint of hardware, Python, Rust, installed dependencies, the requirements file, and thread settings. Changed hardware or environments therefore produce separate series. Environment descriptions are retained in the archive's metadata/ directory.

GitHub-hosted runners share infrastructure and can vary in load and performance. Use the charts as trends, inspect raw samples before drawing conclusions, and reproduce important changes locally. Timing changes do not fail CI.

To deliberately update the pinned environment, recompile it and rerun correctness and smoke checks:

uv pip compile pyproject.toml --group benchmark --extra hdf5 --extra zarr --python-version 3.12 \
  --universal --output-file benchmarks/requirements.txt --no-annotate --upgrade

docs.title: First GitHub Pages deployment
docs.text:
After these files are on main:

  1. In repository Settings > Pages, choose GitHub Actions as the publishing source.
  2. In Actions > Benchmarks > Run workflow, select main and enable initialize_history for the first run.
  3. After it succeeds, follow the deployment URL for documentation, or open its benchmarks/ subdirectory for charts.

The workflow builds documentation in an isolated environment and publishes both sites in one artifact. Existing sites migrate without reinitialization: leave initialize_history disabled to restore the root history archive.

Normal runs leave initialize_history disabled. Main pushes and the weekly Sunday 00:00 UTC schedule benchmark the checked-out main revision and publish the site. Re-running a revision replaces its measurements for that environment; each Actions run also keeps its own recovery artifact. PRs run read-only correctness, discovery, and quick smoke checks without deploying. Manual runs on other branches also perform smoke checks only. History begins with the first run; older revisions are not automatically backfilled.

docs.title: History preservation and recovery
docs.text:
The workflow restores asv-results.tar.gz from the live Pages site before benchmarking. After a successful run it publishes a complete replacement archive containing raw ASV JSON, machine records, and environment descriptions. The whole restore/run/deploy cycle is serialized. No result branches, Git commits, PRs, or external storage are used.

Missing, inaccessible, malformed, or incomplete archives stop publication, leaving the previously deployed site intact. Initialization accepts only a missing archive and no prior successful Pages deployment; it never bypasses corruption. Each publication attempt uploads a benchmark-history-<run id>-<attempt> Actions artifact, retained for 90 days. This is a recovery copy; the live Pages archive is the durable source between runs.

If the published archive is lost or damaged, find a successful main run of Benchmarks with a retained recovery artifact. Run Benchmarks manually on main, leave initialization disabled, and enter that run's numeric ID in recovery_run_id. The workflow verifies the source, restores its archive, benchmarks the current main revision, and republishes the site. Leave recovery blank again for subsequent runs.

To inspect a downloaded recovery archive locally, restore it into an empty history directory and rebuild:

.asv/runner/bin/python scripts/benchmark_history.py restore --archive /path/to/asv-results.tar.gz
.asv/runner/bin/python scripts/benchmark_history.py check
.asv/runner/bin/python -m asv publish
.asv/runner/bin/python scripts/benchmark_history.py pack

Do not initialize a replacement empty database after results have been published.

docs.title: imzML backend benchmark
docs.text:
Recorded on 2026-10-26. These are local warm-cache measurements, not universal speed guarantees.

Machine: arm64, 10 logical CPUs, macOS-27.0.1-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O. Python 3.14.0, NumPy 2.4.6, rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13). Rust release build, default Rayon worker count.

python scripts/benchmark_imzml.py --pixels 4096 --points 2048 --targets 32 --repeats 5 --output benchmark.json

Both datasets contain varied lognormal float32 intensities. The continuous profile dataset shares a float64 axis with 2048 samples. Processed centroid spectra have independent sorted float64 axes with 1024-2048 samples. Random reads select 1024 pixels with replacement. One ion image uses m/z 150; batch extraction uses 32 masses between 150 and 950. Both use a 0.3 Da tolerance.

Times are medians of five runs per backend, with alternating order. Data generation, metadata parsing, correctness checks, and Numba warmup are excluded. Numba JIT is enabled. Every timed spectrum consumes both complete arrays; images and TICs are also consumed. TIC caching is reset on every call. Complete spectra, ion tables, and TIC vectors are checked against the Python implementation before timing. OS file pages are warm; no cold-storage claim is made.

Dataset Operation Python (ms) Rust (ms) Speedup continuous_profile random_spectra 42.810 3.956 10.82x continuous_profile iterate 67.206 13.457 4.99x continuous_profile image 58.497 0.586 99.88x continuous_profile images 227.607 1.972 115.42x continuous_profile tic 61.278 1.675 36.59x processed_centroid random_spectra 40.116 4.198 9.56x processed_centroid iterate 28.533 14.688 1.94x processed_centroid image 30.555 1.797 17.00x processed_centroid images 58.362 4.421 13.20x processed_centroid tic 21.425 2.281 9.39x

Raw timings, input sizes, and pixel throughput are in imzml-macos-arm64.json.
